questions.question: In mutation testing, what is the 'ground string'?

options.A: The original, unmodified program or software artifact under test.
options.B: A string of zeros in memory.
options.C: The text of the mutation operator.

questions.explanation: The ground string P is the original program (or grammar/specification) before any mutation operators are applied.

questions.question: What is a 'mutant' in mutation testing?

options.A: A modified version of the ground string program created by applying a single syntactic change (mutation operator).

questions.explanation: A mutant P' is a syntactically valid program that differs from the original program P by a small syntactic modification introduced by a mutation operator.

questions.question: When is a mutant said to be 'strongly killed' by a test case t?

options.A: When the observable output of the mutant differs from the observable output of the original program: P'(t) ≠ P(t).
options.B: When the mutant crashes the computer.
options.C: When the compiler rejects the mutant.
options.D: When the test case is executed twice.

questions.explanation: Strongly killing a mutant requires that the test case produces a different final output on the mutant compared to the original program (Reachability + Infection + Propagation).

questions.question: When is a mutant said to be 'weakly killed' by a test case t?

options.A: When execution reaches the mutated statement and immediately causes an infected (differing) internal program state, regardless of whether it propagates to the final output.
options.B: When the test runs with low CPU priority.
options.C: When the mutant produces the same output as the original program.
options.D: When the mutant is killed on only 1 operating system.

questions.explanation: Weak mutation requires only Reachability and Infection: the internal execution state immediately following the mutated statement must differ between P and P'.

questions.question: What is an 'equivalent mutant'?

options.A: A mutant that has different syntax but always produces the exact same output behavior as the original program for all possible inputs.
options.B: A mutant that has the same file size.
options.C: A mutant created by two different programmers.
options.D: A mutant with identical line numbers.

questions.explanation: An equivalent mutant is semantically identical to the original program. No test case can ever kill an equivalent mutant because its output never differs from the original.

questions.question: What is the formula for Mutation Score (MS) in mutation testing?

options.A: MS = K / (M - E), where K = killed mutants, M = total mutants, and E = equivalent mutants.

questions.explanation: Mutation Score represents the percentage of non-equivalent mutants killed by the test suite: K / (M - E). If MS = 1.0 (100%), the test suite is mutation-adequate.

questions.question: Why is the Equivalent Mutant Problem known to be fundamentally undecidable in general software engineering?

options.A: Because deciding whether two arbitrary programs compute identical functions is equivalent to the Halting Problem (Rice's Theorem).
options.B: Because mutants are deleted after compilation.
options.C: Because compilers do not support math.
options.D: Because test suites are always finite.

questions.explanation: Determining semantic equivalence between two arbitrary programs is undecidable in general computability theory (Rice's theorem / Halting problem).

questions.question: What are the two core fundamental hypotheses underlying mutation testing?

options.A: The Competent Programmer Hypothesis and the Coupling Effect Hypothesis
options.B: The Halting Hypothesis and Church-Turing Thesis

questions.explanation: Mutation testing rests on: (1) Competent Programmer Hypothesis (programmers write code close to correct, so faults are small syntactic slips) and (2) Coupling Effect (tests that kill simple faults also detect complex faults).

questions.question: What does the 'Coupling Effect' hypothesis state?

options.A: Complex faults are coupled to simple faults in such a way that a test suite capable of detecting all simple first-order mutants will detect the vast majority of complex faults.
options.B: Hardware and software must be tightly coupled.
options.C: Two classes that call each other cannot be tested.
options.D: Mutants must be tested in pairs.

questions.explanation: The Coupling Effect asserts that simple single-token mutations simulate fundamental flaws so well that test suites killing them are sufficiently thorough to catch complex, multi-point bugs.

questions.question: Consider the method 'int Min(int A, int B) { if (A < B) return A; else return B; }'. If mutant 1 changes 'A < B' to 'A <= B', is this an equivalent mutant?

options.A: Yes! When A < B, both return A. When A > B, both return B. When A == B, original returns B (=A) and mutant returns A (=B). Their output is identical for all inputs!
options.B: No, it is killed by input (3, 3).
options.C: No, it is killed by input (2, 5).

questions.explanation: When A == B, returning A vs returning B produces the exact same numerical result. For all other inputs, the branch outcome is identical. Thus the mutant is semantically equivalent!

questions.question: For the same Min method 'if (A < B) return A; else return B;', suppose mutant 2 changes 'A < B' to 'A > B'. Which test input kills this mutant strongly?

options.D: No test case can kill it.

questions.explanation: With (2, 5): Original checks 2 < 5 (True) and returns 2. Mutant checks 2 > 5 (False) and returns 5. Since 2 ≠ 5, the mutant is strongly killed!

questions.question: What is a 'First-Order Mutant' versus a 'Higher-Order Mutant'?

options.A: A First-Order mutant has exactly one mutation applied; a Higher-Order mutant has two or more mutations applied simultaneously.
options.B: First-Order mutants are for Java; Higher-Order are for Python.

questions.explanation: First-Order Mutants (FOM) introduce exactly one mutation per program instance. Higher-Order Mutants (HOM) combine two or more mutations in a single program copy.

questions.question: What is the primary computational bottleneck of mutation testing in continuous integration pipelines?

options.A: The large number of mutants generated, requiring running the test suite hundreds or thousands of times (one per mutant).
options.D: It consumes all hard drive storage permanently.

questions.explanation: Mutation generates O(Lines × Operators) mutants. Running the test suite against every single mutant is computationally expensive ('do-fewer, do-faster, do-smarter' optimizations are used).

questions.question: How does 'weak mutation' achieve significant performance speedups over 'strong mutation'?

options.A: It checks state infection immediately after the mutated statement inside the same execution run without executing the rest of the program.
options.B: It deletes all assertions from tests.
options.C: It skips running the original program.
options.D: It only tests 1 mutant per repository.

questions.explanation: Weak mutation monitors whether the state is infected right after the mutated statement executes. This avoids running the rest of the program or propagating to the end, enabling fast in-process checks.

questions.question: If a test suite executes 100 mutants, kills 80, and 10 are proven to be equivalent mutants, what is the Mutation Score?
What is a 'stillborn mutant' in mutation testing?

options.A: A mutant that cannot even be compiled or syntactically parsed.
options.B: A mutant that kills the operating system.
options.D: A mutant that passes all tests.

questions.explanation: A stillborn mutant is syntactically invalid or fails compilation; modern mutation tools only generate valid mutants that successfully compile.

questions.question: What is a 'trivial mutant'?

options.A: A mutant that is killed by almost any test case that reaches it.
options.B: A mutant that cannot be killed.

questions.explanation: Trivial mutants are very easy to kill (e.g. replacing a return value with null or crashing on entry), providing little discriminative value for test quality.

questions.question: Why is mutation testing considered the 'gold standard' for evaluating test suite quality?

options.A: Because it directly measures the test suite's ability to detect synthetic faults, exposing deficiencies that code coverage metrics miss.
options.B: Because it requires no programming skills.
options.C: Because it is required by HTML5.
options.D: Because it guarantees zero lines of code.

questions.explanation: High line/branch coverage does not guarantee assertions are thorough. Mutation testing measures whether test assertions actually catch deliberate bugs, revealing gaps in test oracles.

questions.question: What is 'mutant subsumption'?

options.A: Mutant m1 subsumes mutant m2 if any test case that kills m1 is guaranteed to also kill m2.
options.B: When a mutant deletes another mutant.

questions.explanation: If killing m1 always implies killing m2, m1 is strictly harder to kill and subsumes m2. Subsumption helps identify minimal sets of non-redundant mutants.

questions.question: In mutation testing, what is 'test suite minimization' based on mutant kills?

options.A: Finding a minimal subset of test cases that kills all killable mutants.

questions.explanation: By framing test selection as a set-cover problem over killed mutants, one can identify the smallest subset of tests that maintains 100% mutation score.
